citation.title: The Effect of Periodization and Training Intensity Distribution on Middle- and Long-Distance Running Performance: A Systematic Review
citation.authors: Mark Kenneally, Arturo Casado, Jordan Santos-Concejero

entries.population: Middle- and long-distance runners represented in 16 observational, case, intervention, and review studies
entries.training_status: Mixed runner populations, with substantial representation from trained and high-performing runners
entries.intervention: Pyramidal, polarized, and threshold training-intensity distributions over at least four weeks
entries.comparison: Comparison between intensity-distribution approaches and their organization relative to goal-race pace
outcomes: Pyramidal and polarized distributions generally produced better performance outcomes than threshold-dominant training
Organizing intensity relative to goal-race pace can coexist with different periodization models
limitations: Only 16 studies met inclusion criteria and study designs were heterogeneous
The included studies had a mean PEDro quality score of 3.75 out of 10
Some successful marathon runners used threshold-oriented training despite the overall review finding
The review does not establish one exact low-intensity percentage for every recreational runner
entries.planning_implication: Keep most running at low intensity, limit demanding sessions, and treat the exact distribution boundaries as policy choices rather than universal constants.

citation.title: Block periodization of endurance training: a systematic review and meta-analysis
citation.authors: Knut Sindre Mølmen, Sjur Johansen Øfsteng, Bent R Rønnestad

entries.population: Trained to well-trained athletes across 20 included studies, including endurance and team-sport populations
entries.intervention: Concentrated endurance-focused training blocks lasting at least one week
entries.comparison: Traditional periodization or athletes' ordinary training
outcomes: Meta-analysis found small favorable effects for maximal oxygen uptake and maximal power
Several endurance and threshold outcomes favored block periodization
limitations: Most included studies were small and of low methodological quality
Prediction intervals included uncertain effects across study settings
The evidence was not specific to recreational half-marathon preparation
entries.planning_implication: Use progressive phases for a single race peak, but do not require concentrated block periodization or claim it is superior for this population.

citation.title: Individualized Endurance Training Based on Recovery and Training Status in Recreational Runners
citation.authors: Olli-Pekka Nuuttila, Ari Nummela, Elisa Korhonen, Keijo Häkkinen, Heikki Kyröläinen

entries.population: Thirty recreational male and female runners in predefined and individualized groups
entries.intervention: Training load adjusted twice weekly from nocturnal heart-rate variability, perceived recovery, and a heart-rate-to-running-speed index
entries.comparison: A predefined 15-week program with the same preparatory, volume, and interval periods
outcomes: Both groups improved maximal treadmill speed and 10-km performance
The individualized group improved 10-km time more and had more high responders and fewer low responders
limitations: The sample was small and the intervention combined several monitoring signals
The adjustment algorithm cannot be reduced to one wearable score
The study does not validate automatic day-to-day schedule changes for every runner
entries.planning_implication: Preserve recovery opportunities and make later plan revisions possible, but do not silently alter the deterministic plan from a single recovery signal.

citation.title: Effects of tapering on performance in endurance athletes: A systematic review and meta-analysis
citation.authors: Zhiqiang Wang, Yong Tai Wang, Weifeng Gao, Yaping Zhong

entries.population: 174 endurance athletes across 14 studies, mainly runners and cyclists and mostly males
entries.training_status: At least well-trained; inclusion required VO2max above 55 mL/kg/min or an equivalent study classification
entries.intervention: Step or progressive tapers lasting up to 21 days
entries.comparison: Pre-taper performance and control or conventional-taper conditions where available
outcomes: Tapering improved time-trial and time-to-exhaustion performance
Subgroups reducing volume by 41-60 percent while maintaining intensity and frequency improved time-trial performance
limitations: Sports, event distances, and taper protocols varied
Only 14 studies and 174 athletes were included
Participants were mostly male and the review did not establish effects for less-trained recreational runners
The result does not identify one uniquely optimal taper for recreational half-marathon runners
entries.planning_implication: Use a one-to-three-week taper that reduces volume substantially while retaining the normal core-session rhythm and small doses of intensity.

citation.title: The Association Between Running Injuries and Training Parameters: A Systematic Review
citation.authors: Anny Fredette, Jean-Sébastien Roy, Kadija Perreault, Frédérique Dupuis, Christopher Napier, Jean-Francois Esculier

entries.population: Novice, recreational, competitive, and mixed runner cohorts in prospective studies and randomized trials
entries.intervention: Different running distances, durations, frequencies, intensities, and recent changes in those parameters
entries.comparison: Injured and uninjured runners or different training progressions
outcomes: Evidence linking distance, duration, frequency, intensity, or recent changes to running-related injury was conflicting
The review found no justification for a universal ten-percent weekly progression rule
limitations: Injury definitions, runner populations, and follow-up periods were highly heterogeneous
The evidence could not support universal progression recommendations
entries.planning_implication: Use conservative progression boundaries as transparent product assumptions and never present them as proven injury-prevention thresholds.

citation.title: An empirical study of race times in recreational endurance runners
citation.authors: Andrew J Vickers, Emily A Vertosick

entries.population: 2303 recreational endurance runners reporting training and race results
entries.intervention: Prediction models using prior race performance, demographics, and routinely available training information
entries.comparison: Riegel race-equivalence predictions and models fitted on a training cohort and checked on a validation cohort
outcomes: Race distance, prior performance, and training information contributed to race-time prediction
The study evaluated a Riegel fatigue exponent of 1.07 and showed that training mileage can improve longer-race estimates
limitations: Training and race information was self-reported through an internet survey
A race-equivalence estimate assumes comparable preparation and conditions
Population estimates do not provide a guaranteed individual result
entries.planning_implication: Use a 1.07 race-equivalence estimate as a transparent baseline, widen it by evidence quality, and keep training-readiness adjustments bounded.

citation.title: Physiological Indicators of Trail Running Performance: A Systematic Review
citation.authors: Arthur de Waal, Reinout Wiersma, Marco Mensink

entries.population: Trail runners in races from 7 to 65 kilometres across seven included studies
entries.training_status: Mixed recreational and trained trail runners
entries.comparison: Associations between indicators and real-world trail-running performance
outcomes: Aerobic capacity, lactate threshold, velocity at aerobic capacity, and running economy were commonly associated with trail performance
limitations: Only seven heterogeneous studies were included
Associations do not identify one optimal training prescription
entries.planning_implication: Retain mostly aerobic training while adding course-specific climbing and terrain exposure.

citation.title: Downhill Running: What Are The Effects and How Can We Adapt? A Narrative Review

entries.population: Healthy and trained runners represented in downhill-running studies
entries.intervention: Downhill running and repeated downhill exposure
entries.comparison: Different gradients, durations, speeds, and prior exposure
outcomes: Downhill running creates eccentric muscle damage influenced by slope, speed, and duration
Prior downhill exposure can reduce later muscle-damage responses
limitations: The review was narrative and protocols were heterogeneous
Many studies used small samples and laboratory descents
entries.planning_implication: Introduce controlled downhill exposure progressively and remove demanding descents from the taper.

citation.title: Injury Prevention, Safe Training Techniques, Rehabilitation, and Return to Sport in Trail Runners
citation.authors: Hollie K. Vincent and Kevin R. Vincent

entries.population: Trail runners and related off-road running populations represented in the reviewed literature
entries.intervention: Terrain practice, neuromotor training, strengthening, and downhill technique considerations
entries.comparison: Injury patterns and proposed prevention strategies across trail-running settings
outcomes: Lower-leg injuries and ankle sprains are important trail-running concerns
Practising similar terrain supports trail-specific movement adaptation
limitations: Much of the trail-specific injury evidence is observational
Several prevention recommendations extrapolate from related sports
entries.planning_implication: Require regular race-like terrain exposure while keeping technical progression explicit and conservative.
